title: Understanding Marketing Metrics
description: CTR, CPC, CPA, conversion rate and ROAS: learn what each one means, match them to definitions, complete the formulas, and see how they move together in a simulator. All figures are illustrative.
objectives: Define CTR, CPC, CPA, conversion rate and ROAS
Calculate each metric from campaign data
Explain how spend, CPC and conversion rate drive CPA
Reason about budget allocation with ROAS

modules.title: Metric deck
modules.instructions: Eight metrics every Brightline Media account runs on. Flip, then rate yourself honestly.

cards.back:
**Cost per mille** — what you pay for 1,000 ad impressions.

Spend ÷ impressions × 1,000.
cards.hint: The *M* is the Roman numeral for a thousand.

cards.back:
**Cost per click** — average spend for one click on the ad.

Spend ÷ clicks.

**Click-through rate** — the share of impressions that turned into clicks.

Clicks ÷ impressions. A relevance signal for the creative.
cards.hint: It compares two counts and never looks at spend.

cards.back:
**Cost per acquisition** — what one conversion (lead, signup, sale) costs.

Spend ÷ conversions.

**Return on ad spend** — revenue earned for every unit of spend.

Revenue ÷ spend. A ROAS of 3.4× means €3.40 back per €1.

**Lifetime value** — the total revenue (or margin) a customer brings over the whole relationship.

Used to decide how high a CPA you can afford.

**Conversion rate** — the share of visitors who completed the goal.

Conversions ÷ clicks (or sessions). A landing-page signal.

**Average order value** — revenue divided by the number of orders.

Raising AOV lifts ROAS without buying more traffic.

feedback.complete: Deck done. Those eight metrics cover almost every conversation you'll have with a client.

modules.title: Match the metric to its meaning
modules.instructions: Tap a metric, then tap its definition — or drag the metric onto the definition. Fewer mistakes, higher score.

pairs.explanation: Cost per mille. A CPM of $8 means every thousand impressions cost $8 — useful for comparing reach-focused placements.
Cost per click. Spend ÷ clicks. The Northwind Outdoor account averages $1.40 on search and $0.62 on social.

pairs.right: Share of impressions that turned into clicks
pairs.explanation: Click-through rate. Clicks ÷ impressions. A 2% CTR means 2 clicks for every 100 impressions.

pairs.right: What one acquisition (lead or sale) costs
pairs.explanation: Cost per acquisition. Spend ÷ conversions. It is the efficiency metric most clients care about.

pairs.right: Revenue earned for every unit of ad spend
pairs.explanation: Return on ad spend. Revenue ÷ spend. A ROAS of 4.0 means $4 of revenue for every $1 spent.

pairs.right: Average number of times one person saw the ad
pairs.explanation: Impressions ÷ reach. When frequency climbs past 4–5 on social, creative fatigue usually follows.

pairs.right: Number of unique people who saw the ad
pairs.explanation: Unlike impressions, reach counts each person once — the right metric for awareness goals.

pairs.right: Share of visitors who completed the goal
pairs.explanation: Conversions ÷ clicks (or sessions). A high CTR with a low conversion rate points at the landing page, not the ad.

feedback.complete: You now speak fluent media metrics. The explanations below are worth a second read.

modules.title: Complete the metric formulas
modules.instructions: Tap a word to drop it into the next blank. Tap a filled blank to put the word back.

content.template: **ROAS** is revenue divided by {{roas}}, so a ROAS of 3.4× means every dollar brought back $3.40. **CPA** is spend divided by the number of {{cpa}} — it tells you what each result cost. **CTR** is {{clicks}} divided by {{impressions}}, which makes it a quick read on how relevant an ad is to the people who saw it.

blanks.hint: ROAS stands for *return on ad spend* — the denominator is in the name.
blanks.explanation: ROAS = revenue ÷ ad spend. It ignores margin, so pair it with CPA when judging profitability.

blanks.hint: The *A* in CPA is the outcome you pay for: a purchase, a sign-up, a lead.
blanks.explanation: CPA = spend ÷ conversions. Define what counts as a conversion before comparing campaigns.

blanks.hint: You can only click an ad after it has been shown — that showing has a name.
blanks.explanation: CTR = clicks ÷ impressions. A CTR of 2.8% means 28 clicks for every 1,000 impressions.

content.explanation: ROAS tells you how much revenue each unit of spend returned, CPA tells you what each result cost, and CTR tells you how often people who saw the ad clicked it. Together they describe return, efficiency and relevance.

feedback.correct: Those are the three formulas every Brightline account manager should know by heart.
feedback.complete: Nice — you can now read a Pulse Analytics overview without a glossary.

modules.title: Metric myths
modules.instructions: Eight quick calls. Swipe right for true, left for false, or use the buttons.

statements.text: CTR is calculated as clicks divided by impressions.
statements.explanation: Correct. CTR compares two counts and never involves spend, which makes it a creative-relevance signal.

statements.text: A lower ROAS is always better for the client.
statements.explanation: ROAS is revenue ÷ spend, so higher means more revenue per euro. Lower ROAS means the campaign returns less.

statements.text: CPM tells you what 1,000 impressions cost.
statements.explanation: Yes. The *M* stands for mille: spend ÷ impressions × 1,000.

statements.text: If CTR is high but CVR is low, the ads are probably the problem.
statements.explanation: A high CTR shows the ads earn clicks. A low CVR after the click points to the landing page or the offer, not the creative.

statements.text: LTV helps you decide how high a CPA you can afford.
statements.explanation: Exactly. If a customer is worth €400 over their lifetime, a €60 CPA may be fine; if they're worth €50, it isn't.

statements.text: Raising AOV lowers ROAS because customers spend more.
statements.explanation: The opposite. More revenue per order on the same spend pushes ROAS up.

statements.text: CPA is spend divided by the number of conversions.
statements.explanation: Right. It's the most direct efficiency metric for an acquisition campaign.

statements.text: Doubling the budget on a campaign will double its conversions.
statements.explanation: Audiences saturate and auctions get pricier. Expect CPA to rise as spend scales, which is why we scale in steps and watch the number.

feedback.complete: Myths busted. These are the eight mistakes we see most often in client decks.

modules.title: Acquisition cost explorer
modules.instructions: Drag the sliders to see how budget, bidding and conversion rate shape the cost of every new customer for a fictional paid-search campaign.

inputs.label: Monthly ad spend
inputs.help: Total media budget for the month.

inputs.label: Cost per click (CPC)
inputs.help: Average price paid for one click. Rises with competition and falls with better ad relevance.

inputs.label: Conversion rate
inputs.help: Share of visitors who become customers. Landing-page quality moves this most.

inputs.label: Average order value
inputs.help: Revenue from a typical first order.

outputs.label: Cost per acquisition (CPA)
outputs.help: What one new customer costs: spend ÷ conversions.

insights.text: Each customer costs more than they spend on their first order. Lower the CPC, lift the conversion rate, or raise the order value before scaling budget.
ROAS of **3× or more** — every dollar of spend returns at least three in revenue. This is the zone where adding budget usually pays off.
A CPC above $4 points to crowded auctions or a low Quality Score. Tighter keywords and more relevant ad copy tend to bring it down.

challenge.description: Bring **CPA under $30** while keeping spend at or above **$10,000**.
challenge.successMessage: You found a profitable mix. Notice that conversion rate and CPC move CPA far more than raw budget does — budget only scales whatever efficiency you already have.

modules.title: Allocate the budget
modules.instructions: Illustrative numbers from two channels in the same month.

questions.prompt: Search: $10,000 spend, $42,000 revenue. Social: $10,000 spend, $18,000 revenue. The client adds $5,000. Where does it go?
questions.context: ROAS — Search 4.2×, Social 1.8×. Assume both channels still have headroom.

options.explanation: With headroom, the higher-ROAS channel earns the marginal dollar.
Even splits feel fair but ignore the 2.4× difference in return.

options.text: All of it to Social, to help it catch up
options.explanation: Spending more on the weaker channel does not make it stronger.

questions.explanation: Marginal budget follows marginal return — until the stronger channel runs out of headroom.

questions.prompt: Which metrics would you watch to notice that Search has run out of headroom? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: A rising CTR is good news, not a saturation signal.

questions.explanation: Saturation shows up as more expensive clicks, weaker conversion and flat revenue.
